title: With Uncertainty Shrouding UN Shipping Climate Talks, NGOs Call on Governments to Avoid Backsliding on Ambition
summary: Ahead of MEPC 85, the IMO's already insufficient Net-Zero Framework faces further sabotage from the US and petrostates, threatening any meaningful reduction in shipping's carbon intensity. Despite the unanimous 2023 GHG Strategy, current backsliding risks maintaining reliance on high-carbon fuels and avoiding stricter FuelEU Maritime-style regulations globally. This continued political inaction ensures the dirtiest ships will evade accountability, allowing excessive HFO usage and exceeding CII ratings with impunity.
content:
Ahead of next week’s meeting of the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85, Nov 30-Dec 4), the Clean Shipping Coalition calls on member states to stay true to the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, by ensuring that the strategy’s ambition and commitment to a just & equitable energy transition are translated into an effective framework.

The IMO’s climate ambition came under severe threat during this week’s meeting of the IMO’s Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23 Nov 23-27). Following four days of mostly closed door discussions, indications suggest that pressure from the US and a slew of petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, is threatening the possibility of a fit-for-purpose IMO shipping climate deal. The levels of ambition of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), the IMO’s already approved mechanism for reducing shipping emissions from shipping, are being questioned and weakened.

“After some IMO member states continued to launch attacks on climate ambition this week, the Marine Environment Protection Committee must turn things around”, said Lukas Leppert, President of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “Next week, climate leaders within IMO member states have the singular opportunity of translating the IMO GHG Strategy into action – they must stand shoulder to shoulder, ignore distraction from false solutions and establish a global framework that meets shipping’s obligation to clean-up its climate warming emissions in a manner that leaves no state behind.”

“IMO member states must match the ambition they unanimously agreed to in the IMO’s 2023 GHG strategy; reduce the climate impact of global shipping, which makes up 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, support the uptake of sustainable marine fuels and technologies, agree a financing mechanism for decarbonisation of the sector, and to deliver on a just and equitable energy transition, so that vulnerable countries facing disproportionate impacts are supported in the transition”, added Leppert.

Earlier this week, the Clean Shipping Coalition wrote to José Raúl Mulino Quintero, President of the Republic of Panama, commending Panama’s strong position at COP31, and urging Panama to take a similarly strong stance at the International Maritime Organization.

“Next week, Panama must join others by bringing their COP31 climate leadership to the IMO, by helping ensure the UN’s shipping body enshrines the importance of climate regulation and a just & equitable transition in IMO’s global shipping policies”, said John Maggs, the Clean Shipping Coalition’s Representative at IMO.

“Communities on the frontlines of the climate crisis are fighting for their survival”, said Andrew Dumbrille, Co-Director of Equal Routes. “A global climate framework for shipping must centre their rights and support their economies. The just and equitable transition that IMO Member States committed to in the 2023 GHG Strategy cannot remain a promise on paper. It needs to be put into practice to support those most impacted by the climate crisis and who have done the least to cause it. There can be no compromise on this.”

“An ambitious global framework for reduction of shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions would establish a level playing field that reduces emissions and drives production of sustainable technologies and fuels”, said Sönke Diesener, Senior Policy Officer Maritime Transport at NABU. “Instead, a framework weak in ambition and impact rises will result in a fragmentation of shipping’s climate regulation with a multitude of national and regional regulations filling the gaps. IMO member states should deliver on the chance of harmonized regulation of shipping’s climate heating emissions instead of fragmentation.”

“The lack of progress this week shows that many countries are unwilling to accept proposals that would lower ambition or put the IMO’s GHG strategy goals out of reach; shipping cannot afford more delays in tackling its climate pollution”, said Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director at Ocean Conservancy. “When negotiations resume next week, IMO member states must come prepared to deliver a strong framework that cuts emissions, provides industry certainty and funds for a transition for the countries most at risk. There is simply too much at stake to keep kicking the can down the road.”

“After drawn-out discussions and slow progress, it is more important than ever to recall the climate goals of the IMO and its member states”, said Felix Klann, Shipping Policy Officer at T&E. “If IMO member states cannot deliver on their obligations, additional action is needed to fill the gaps, not only on setting targets, but in providing incentives and investments in clean fuels and technologies.”
